etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English fo (“foe; hostile”), from earlier ifo (“foe”), from Old English ġefāh (“enemy”), from fāh (“hostile”), from Proto-West Germanic *faih, from Proto-Germanic *faihaz (compare Old Frisian fāch (“punishable”), Middle High German gevēch (“feuder”)), from Proto-Indo-European *peyk/ḱ- (“to hate, be hostile”) (compare Middle Irish óech (“enemy, fiend”), Lithuanian pìktas (“evil”)).

quote.citation: 2013 June 29, “Travels and travails”, in The Economist, volume 407, number 8842, page 55:
quote.text: Even without hovering drones, a lurking assassin, a thumping score and a denouement, the real-life story of Edward Snowden, a rogue spy on the run, could be straight out of the cinema. But, as with Hollywood, the subplots and exotic locations may distract from the real message: America’s discomfort and its foes’ glee.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Acronym of [ten to the power of] fifty-one ergs, due to equalling 10 ergs; coined by Gerald Brown of Stony Brook University in his work with Hans Bethe.

definitions.definition: A unit of energy equal to 1044 joules.
